paper_r0.quote: suggesting weakly selective aggregation into a small feature space
paper_r0.say: The model says the outlined head L0H4 barely chooses what to look at, because its Choose weights are tiny, 0.009 against 0.97 for L0H5. So it likely reads everything about equally and writes a short blended summary.

paper_r0.quote: consistent with two-characters-back and previous-character heads, respectively
paper_r0.say: The model says L0H5 likely looks one character back and L0H1 two back, and stresses that these distances are inferred. Patterns in their Choose weights suggest L0H1 steps back about twice as far as L0H5.

paper_r0.quote: This key-specific matching supports successor/context-copying circuits
paper_r0.say: The model says L2H1, L3H1 and L3H5 may be copying heads. Copying means finding an earlier match and repeating what came next. What earlier heads write suits how these heads choose, in one order only, which supports copying without proving it.

check.note: Recomputed 0.0776, 0.1104, 0.1836; the 14 strongest of 216 head pairs all end in true copying heads 2.1, 3.1 or 3.5.

paper_r0.quote: This suggests shared positional routing, but does not independently establish locality.
paper_r0.say: The model says L1H1 to L1H5 likely share one way of choosing by position. Over half of their key weights read L0H4's short summary, so they seem to steer by the same signal. It adds that this alone does not show they look nearby.

check.note: Recomputed shares 52.5% to 67.8%; true mean look-back of L1H1 to L1H5 is 1.8 to 2.6.

paper_r0.quote: L2H2: unclear — important precursor to both late copy candidates
paper_r0.say: The model leaves L2H2 unclear. It calls L2H2 an important feeder of both late copying candidates, L3H1 and L3H5, because what it writes suits how they choose. It could not verify how far L2H2 itself looks.

check.note: The two feeding links are the top pairs (0.1836, 0.1104), yet 'unclear' misses a strong previous-character head: prev 0.628, dist 1.8.

paper_r0.say: The model labels L2H1, L3H1 and L3H5 as copying heads, with L3H5 the strongest candidate. L3H5's choosing lines up with what L2H2 writes at 0.18, well ahead of 0.11 for L3H1.

check.note: Exactly the three heads above 0.2: 2.1 (0.245), 3.1 (0.269), 3.5 (0.546), with 3.5 truly the highest; no false labels.

paper_r0.quote: favor as-is text substantially over independently shuffled lines
paper_r0.say: The model favors as-is text over independently shuffled lines, at 0.96. It points to the heads that likely look a short fixed distance back and to the one-way copying links.

paper_r0.say: The model weakly favors Python, at 0.56 against 0.31 for English. Repeated names and code fragments would give copying heads plenty to do. It stresses that these circuits are not specific to code and that it recovered no letters or keywords.

check.note: The true text is Python; the model gave it 0.56, against 0.31 for English.

paper_r1.quote: This suggests related positional offsets—plausibly two-back and one-back.
paper_r1.say: The model says L0H5 plausibly looks one character back and L0H1 two back. Applying L0H5's Choose pattern twice resembles L0H1 better than applying it once, as a two-step hop would. Exact distances stay uncertain.

paper_r1.quote: It appears to aggregate a few shared features rather than select individual characters sharply.

paper_r1.quote: These are substantial learned alignments, although they do not alone prove behavioral induction.

check.note: Recomputed 0.0776, 0.1104, 0.1836 against control spread 0.0027; the three target heads are the true copying heads.

paper_r1.quote: L1H1: local — Strong key-bias norm 3.150 and shared alignment 0.965; likely strongly recency-biased.

paper_r1.quote: L2H2: local — Strong shared bias alignment, 0.904; especially important as a source for later copy-like matching.

check.note: Exactly the three heads above 0.2: 2.1 (0.245), 3.1 (0.269), 3.5 (0.546); no false labels.

paper_r1.quote: The offset-like early machinery and multiple strong matching compositions favor preserved character order
paper_r1.say: The model favors preserved character order over independently shuffled lines, at 0.99. It points to the early heads that seem to look a fixed distance back and to several strong matching links.

check.note: The training text was used as is; the model gave that 0.99.

paper_r1.quote: Python is my slight corpus favorite

astra.quote: L0H1 aligns with the square of L0H5’s rotational operator

astra.say: The model says L0H4 likely blends what it sees without picking much out. Its Choose weights are tiny, 0.074 against 7.764 for L0H5, while its Write weights stay strong and pass on a short summary.

astra.say: The model says L2H1, L3H1 and L3H5 likely copy, meaning they find an earlier match and repeat what came next. What L0H5 writes lines up with how they choose, about 0.7 each, and the reverse order scores negative.

check.note: Rerun gives 0.719, 0.666, 0.705, the top three of 18 heads (next is 0.305); these are the only true copying heads (0.245, 0.269, 0.546).

astra.quote: L3H1 and L3H5 also have aligned token-to-output weight maps

astra.quote: This weakly favors a fully used Latin alphabet over predominantly Hepburn romaji.
astra.say: The model weakly leans away from romaji. With position-like weights set aside, the Read weights of L0H1 and L0H5 stay strong through 27 signals, then drop, which hints at a full alphabet. It says no letters were identified.

check.note: Rerun gives 1.379, 1.301, 0.832 at places 26 to 28; the text is Python and uses all 28 characters, the rarest (j) at 0.15%.

astra.say: The model tentatively says L2H2 looks at the previous character. How it chooses lines up with L0H5's writing in the opposite order from the copying heads, 0.66 against -0.48.

astra.quote: Multiple copying circuits make Python my narrow preference

astra_r1.quote: L0H1 aligns with the square of L0H5’s polar factor
astra_r1.say: The model says L0H5 likely looks one character back and L0H1 two back, while exact distances stay unknown. L0H5's Choose pattern applied twice resembles L0H1, 0.64 against 0.07 applied once.

astra_r1.quote: This strongly suggests broad, low-dimensional aggregation.

check.note: Rerun gives 0.009, 0.970 and 17.158; true mean look-back of L0H4 is 32.0 with prev 0.035.

astra_r1.quote: These are substantial matching signatures, not proof of copying behavior.
astra_r1.say: The model says L2H1, L3H1 and L3H5 may copy, meaning they find an earlier match and repeat what came next. What L0H5 and L2H2 write lines up with how they choose, which it says falls short of proof.

astra_r1.quote: That weakly disfavors romaji; spectral rank is not a literal vocabulary count.
astra_r1.say: The model weakly leans away from romaji. The last MLP's output weights stay strong across many signals, from 20 down to about 8, so it sees no tight limit on characters. It warns this is no letter count.

check.note: Rerun gives 20.293, 10.769, 7.929; at place 28 the Python network has 7.93, English 7.17 and romaji 4.58, so this measure does separate romaji.

astra_r1.quote: positional routing does not establish locality
astra_r1.say: The model leaves all of L1 unclear. Up to 68% of these heads' key weights read L0H4's summary, so they seem to pick by position, but it says that does not show they look nearby.

check.note: Rerun gives 34.2% to 67.8%; but L1H1 to L1H5 are local (dist 1.8 to 2.6, prev 0.26 to 0.31), so 'unclear' misses a pattern that holds.

astra_r1.quote: L2H2: unclear — its writes strongly support later matching circuits
astra_r1.say: The model leaves L2H2 unclear. What it writes feeds the copying heads strongly, but it says this cannot show where L2H2 itself looks.

check.note: The writing links hold (0.288, 0.390), but L2H2 has prev 0.628 and dist 1.8, so the model missed a clear previous-character head.

astra_r1.say: The model calls L3H5 its strongest copying candidate. How it chooses lines up with L2H2's writing at 0.39 and L0H5's at 0.19.

check.note: Rerun gives 0.390 and 0.187; L3H5 has the highest copying score of all 24 heads, 0.546.

astra_r1.quote: I weakly favor English, with Python a close alternative.
astra_r1.say: The model weakly favors English, 0.50 against 0.35 for Python. Its many character signals weigh somewhat against romaji, and it says nothing it recovered decides between English and Python.

check.note: The true text is Python, given 0.35 against 0.50 for English; python's network has 3 copying heads, English's 1 and romaji's 1.

claude.quote: L0H1 and L0H5 share a positional subspace
claude.say: The model says L0H1 and L0H5 both pick by position, using the same part of their Choose weights. Their overlap is 0.63, against under 0.25 for other pairs in the layer.

check.note: Rerun gives 0.632, the top pair, but two other pairs exceed 0.25: L0H2 with L0H3 at 0.364, L0H0 with L0H3 at 0.263.

claude.say: The model says L0H5 looks one character back and L0H1 two to three back. It turned repeating patterns in their Choose weights into a score by distance, and assumed L0H5's distance of 1 to set the scale.

check.note: Rerun gives 4 / 17 / 4 and an L0H1 peak of 13.1 at offset 2, but offset 1 is assumed; L0H5 fits (prev 0.649), L0H1 has prev 0.058, dist 6.0.

claude.quote: so it is a plain running mean
claude.say: The model says L0H4 simply averages everything before it. Its Choose weights look untouched by training, 2.2 against 2.22 expected from a random start, so they set almost no preference.

check.note: Recomputed sizes 2.17 and 2.62, score form 0.01; true dist 32.0, prev 0.035, though 2.22 appears in no run and K sits above it.

claude.say: The model says the first MLP holds 27 clear character signals, though without letter names. A search of its weights for sharply tuned units found them stable on repeat tries, with 3 weak leftovers.

check.note: Rerun gives 27 values of 41 to 400, then 14, 10, 9; the alphabet has 28 characters, so one was missed. The romaji network gives only 18 above 30.

claude.quote: I scored same-token matches between query and key
claude.say: The model says L2H1, L3H1 and L3H5 copy, meaning they find an earlier match and repeat what came next. Their query and key weights favour the same character one step apart, about 16 against 5.8 for L3H0.

check.note: Rerun gives 16.8, 15.0, 17.1, the top three of 18 heads; these are the three true copying heads (0.245, 0.269, 0.546).

claude.say: The model labels L3H0 a weaker copying head. It scores 5.8 on the matching test and agrees only 0.31 with the strong heads' output.

check.note: Rerun gives 5.8 and 0.31, but L3H0's copying score is 0.018, far below the 0.2 line.

claude.quote: Hepburn romaji should leave l, q, v and x nearly unused
claude.say: The model argues against romaji, which should leave four letters nearly unused and about 24 active characters. It sees 27 in similar use. It adds that a five-character group that looked like vowels stays unconfirmed.

check.note: Its count does separate the networks: 27 sharp signals above 30 for Python, 26 for English, 18 for romaji; the true text is not romaji.

claude.quote: English over Python: This is a weaker call.
claude.say: The model picks English over Python, 0.62 against 0.28, and calls this a weaker call. Copying heads barely use the likely space character, while Python indentation should lean on copying spaces, and it found no frequent newline.

check.note: The true text is Python (spaces 27.8%, newlines 2.3%). Token 23 cannot be confirmed as space, and no network has a copying head in L1, so that point does not discriminate.

claude_r1.say: The model warns that some of its tests came close to the rule against running the network, by clipping how units respond to characters. It asks readers to discount any corpus evidence resting on them.

check.note: The code confirms runs 40 to 46 and 32, but runs 18, 22 to 25 and 27 also pushed character vectors through the MLP, and it does not mention them.

claude_r1.quote: W_proj.3 has exactly 27 dense output directions
claude_r1.say: The model says the last MLP writes into exactly 27 strong output signals, well above the background level of 2.7. It reads a few other sparse ones as adjusting overall scale.

check.note: Rerun gives 20.29 to 7.93, but the next values are 6.50, 5.27, 3.97 before background 2.8, so 27 is no sharp edge; the alphabet has 28.

claude_r1.quote: Their shared modes have complex phases, with H1's about 2.2 times H5's, which fits lags of 1 and 2.
claude_r1.say: The model says L0H5 looks one character back and L0H1 two back, taking L0H5's distance as its starting point. Repeating patterns in L0H1's Choose weights run about 2.2 times as fast as L0H5's.

check.note: Rerun gives near-commuting at 0.092; L0H5 fits (prev 0.649, dist 2.5), L0H1 has prev 0.058, dist 6.0, and truth has no two-back measure.

claude_r1.quote: L0H4 has B≈0 (norm 0.01) and uniform attention.
claude_r1.say: The model says L0H4 pays equal attention to everything, since its Choose weights are almost nil, 0.01. It writes position strongly, and later key weights read that, which it says biases them toward recent characters.

check.note: Rerun gives 0.01 and writing 18.81, 15.37; L0H4 has dist 32.0, and L1 heads are recent, dist 1.8 to 4.4.

claude_r1.quote: I tested whether the query's current character matches the key's lag-1 character
claude_r1.say: The model says L2H1, L3H1 and L3H5 copy, meaning they find an earlier match and repeat what came next. Their query and key weights favour the same character one step apart, about 3 against 1.07 for L3H0.

check.note: Rerun gives 3.10, 2.74, 3.12, the top three of 18; they are the true copying heads, though L3H0, its weak low-confidence pick, is not (0.018).

claude_r1.quote: L2H2: local; coupling 1.45 and an aligned lag-1 match (+3.19), but no shifted match (−1.19).
claude_r1.say: The model says L2H2 looks close by and does not copy. It favours the same character at the same distance, 3.19, but fails the one-step shifted test, -1.19.

check.note: Rerun gives 3.19 and -1.19; L2H2 has copying score 0.000, prev 0.628 and dist 1.8.

claude_r1.quote: all 28 characters are active on both input and output, with no gap near 24
claude_r1.say: The model argues against romaji, which should leave four letters almost unused. It sees all 28 characters active with no gap near 24, and calls this moderate evidence since training can build detectors for rare characters.

check.note: Same test on all three networks: sharp signals above 10 number 27 for Python, 28 for English, 17 for romaji; the true text is not romaji.

claude_r1.quote: The lean to english is weak.
claude_r1.say: The model leans weakly to English, 0.50 against 0.36 for Python. It found no clear indentation sign, and its fit to English was slightly better but within noise.

check.note: The true text is Python, given 0.36 against 0.50 for English; run 44 gives 0.33 against 0.27 with spread 0.10, and romaji scored highest at 0.37.
